As AI democratises drug discovery, the real differentiator may no longer be who can design a molecule, but who can turn it into a medicine.

That was the thread running through a fascinating conversation I had with five accomplished life sciences entrepreneurs at IKMC 2026 in Hyderabad, exploring the convergence of AI and biology.

India has mastered the economics of manufacturing affordable medicines at scale. The opportunity now is to discover, develop and commercialise original therapies.

AI is lowering the barriers to discovery. What it does not necessarily lower are the challenges of experimental validation, clinical development, patient capital, regulation and commercialisation. And nothing in that list is solved by a better model alone.

The harder question is who captures the value. Indian science succeeding is not the same as India benefiting from it.

My thanks to Vijay Chandru, Kavitha Iyer Rodrigues, Sanjay Singh, Anand Anandkumar and Shesheer Kumar for an engaging exchange of perspectives, and to Satya Prakash Dash and the IKP team for bringing us together.

The International Knowledge Millennium Conference (IKMC 2026), held on 23–24 November convened researchers, scientists, clinicians, entrepreneurs, investors, policymakers and industry leaders for engaging conversations and meaningful exchanges.

With the theme “𝗔𝗰𝗰𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲: 𝗔𝗜 𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗙𝗿𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗳 𝗕𝗶𝗼𝘀𝗰𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲, 𝗦𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗲 & 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲,” the conference explored how AI is transforming the life sciences landscape and what it will take for India to lead this emerging frontier.

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗛𝗶𝗴𝗵𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝗜𝗞𝗠𝗖 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲:

🔹 𝗚𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝗛𝗼𝗻𝗼𝘂𝗿: The inaugural plenary featured addresses by Dr Ravindranath Kancherla and Prof. Vijay Chandru, with IKP Chairperson Deepanwita Chattopadhyay and CEO Dr. Satya Prakash Dash setting the context for the conference. Dr. Chandrasekhar Nair delivered the valedictory address on Day 2.
🔹 𝗙𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗧𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵𝘁-𝗣𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗼𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗣𝗮𝗻𝗲𝗹 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗰𝘂𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀: Industry leaders and experts explored AI and the changing landscape of Indian pharma, funding the Product Nation, bridging the gap between research institutions and industry, and navigating strategy, workforce transformation and competitiveness in the age of AI.
🔹 𝗧𝗲𝗰𝗵 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗼 𝗙𝗲𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝟲𝟬 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁𝘂𝗽𝘀: Entrepreneurs showcased emerging technologies and innovative solutions, engaging with industry experts, investors, jury members and delegates.
🔹 𝗧𝘄𝗼 𝗛𝗮𝗻𝗱𝘀-𝗼𝗻 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁𝘂𝗽 𝗖𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗰𝘀 and 𝗧𝘄𝗼 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗿𝘁 𝗥𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲𝘀:
The startup clinics addressed practical challenges in taking medtech innovations from prototype to patient, navigating regulatory pathways and scaling biomanufacturing, while the expert roundtables explored climate resilience and sustainability, and the convergence of food and microbiome science, with a focus on emerging scientific opportunities, policy imperatives and pathways for technology translation.

From scientific discovery and research translation to patient capital, regulatory readiness and manufacturing scale, IKMC 2026 provided a platform to examine the opportunities and challenges that will define India's next phase of innovation-led growth.

As we conclude this edition, we extend our sincere gratitude to all our distinguished speakers, moderators, panellists, mentors, jury members, startups, partners and delegates for their valuable contributions.

As the conversations at IKMC 2026 move beyond the conference room, we look forward to building on the ideas, connections and possibilities that emerged over these two days.

Thank you for being part of IKMC 2026!

In India, approximately 1 billion sanitary napkins are used every month. But what happens to them after they are discarded?

Much of this waste ends up in landfills, while waste pickers often handle it without adequate protection. Addressing this challenge requires safer collection systems and effective waste processing solutions.

PadCaree, founded by Ajinkya Dhariya, is a startup part of the Circular Bharat Accelerator (CBA), an initiative by Hindustan Unilever Limited and NITI Aayog Official in partnership with NSRCEL and Xynteo.

CBA brings together industry, policy, and ecosystem expertise to support startups with go-to-market refinement, pilot access, and pathways to scale.

PadCare is addressing sanitary waste through its collection and recycling system. Its PadCare bins enable the collection of used sanitary napkins, which are then processed using its technology. The cellulose is converted into pulp for making stationery, while the plastic is converted into pellets used to manufacture planter pots and PadCare bins.

By creating a pathway to recover materials from sanitary waste, PadCare is working towards a more sustainable and circular approach to menstrual waste management.

The latest fad on development panels, nowhere more than on innovation, is "ecosystem building". A sector is built when institutions take accountability for the entire continuum from the laboratory to the last-mile customer, absorbing risks markets refuse to underwrite: unproven technologies, uncertain demand, absent financing, missing service networks and policy gaps.

Funders, CSR and foundations alike, back short-term projects and seek attribution for outcomes that take a decade to materialise and belong to many. Civil society often mistakes convening for building. 𝗣𝗹𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘆 𝗼𝗳 𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲𝘀. 𝗩𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗳𝗲𝘄 𝗽𝘂𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗼𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀. "Ecosystem" has become a convenient word that lets everyone participate without anyone being accountable for the outcome. Convening is a tool, not an outcome.

Sectors move when the incentives of the State, markets and communities align, and when institutions with skin in the game stay invested in keeping them aligned long after the programme closes. Ecosystem building is not about bringing stakeholders together. It is about taking responsibility for what happens after they do.

COVID-19 taught us that the world can mobilise extraordinary resources when confronted with an existential threat. Climate change is teaching us that not every existential threat produces the same urgency. 

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝘆 𝗹𝗶𝗲 𝗶𝗻 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗸.

COVID-19 was never democratic in its consequences. The poor and vulnerable suffered disproportionately. But the virus could reach the boardroom as easily as the slum or the farm. Wealth and power offered protection, not immunity.

Climate change is different. Its earliest and harshest consequences fall on those who contributed least to the problem and have the fewest means to protect themselves. A farmer cannot move agriculture indoors. A construction worker cannot air-condition a building site. A poor household cannot insure itself against every disaster and failed harvest. Those with wealth and power, meanwhile, can buy themselves protection and, more importantly, time.

Urgency and resource allocation often reflect the exposure and priorities of the powerful, rather than the scale of suffering.

There are other explanations, of course. COVID was immediate and visible. Climate risks accumulate over decades, even as their consequences are already devastating lives and livelihoods. 

Risk is not just a scientific probability. It is also a political variable, shaped by who is exposed, who can escape, who can afford protection and who has the power to demand action.

𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗸𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗳𝘂𝗹, 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗲𝘀. 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘆 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗹𝗲𝘀𝘀, 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗲𝘀. 𝗘𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗰𝗲𝘀. 𝗗𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗲𝘀 𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝗽𝗮𝗻𝗲𝗹𝘀, 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀, 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲𝘀, 𝗽𝘂𝗯𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀, 𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗿𝘀, 𝗰𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗯𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀.

Which raises an uncomfortable question:

The obstacle to climate action is not that we fail to understand the risk or communicate it. It is that those who allocate resources can afford to postpone its consequences.

PS: I am acutely aware of my own privilege. I can afford almost everything needed to protect myself from the worst consequences of climate change. And I will probably be dead long before the world reaches net zero. That, perhaps, is precisely the problem. I have the luxury of time. Billions do not.

What would it take to enable more dignified livelihoods for India’s waste pickers?

The circular economy is often discussed in terms of how resources can be reduced, reused, recycled and recovered. But if systems are being rebuilt to value materials differently, there is also a need to rethink how the people who collect, sort, recover and transform those materials are valued.

Waste pickers form the invisible backbone of India’s waste management system. Yet the recognition, security and dignity that should come with this work are often missing. A start-up, with the right support, can create formal employment, giving people greater agency, stability, and the opportunity to define their own economic futures.
